item.title: Cyclical high-magnitude lake drainage slows Greenland ice sheet motion
item.dc:creator: Yefan Wang, Peter Nienow, Jaime Otero, Yefan Wang
item.description:
Nature Communications — matched: ice sheet, subglacial, ice dynamics, glacier, Greenland, meltwater
Global glacier recession is driving a rapid increase in the number and volume of ice-marginal lakes, leading to more frequent Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). The long-term impact of GLOFs on glacier dynamics remains poorly understood, including in Greenland, which holds the largest glacial lake volume in the world. Here, using multi-decadal observations from Isortuarsuup Sermia, Southwest Greenland, we reveal that cyclical GLOFs regulate ice sheet motion. We identify a ‘sawtooth’ pattern of ice-dynamics, whereby multi-year acceleration is terminated abruptly by high-magnitude lake-drainage that resets the glacier to a ‘quiescent’ state for several years. The 2022 event exemplifies this process: the near-terminus ice velocity accelerated briefly from a pre-event baseline of ~200 m a −1 to ~1000 m a −1 before dropping to ~50 m a −1 over subsequent years. Each GLOF releases an immense meltwater volume (mean discharge in 2022 ~17000 m³ s −1), carving a ~1.5-km-wide, efficient subglacial channel. This channel enables extensive lowering of the subglacial water pressure, increasing ice–bed friction and suppressing ice motion. As climate warming increases GLOF frequency, this powerful negative feedback will modulate ice sheet motion acting as a brake on ice-dynamics at the margins of the Greenland Ice Sheet.

item.title: West Antarctic ice retreat temporarily halted with transient rheology in future climate projections
item.dc:creator: Allie N. Coonin, B. Parazin, Harriet C. P. Lau, Natalya Gomez
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, Antarctic, West Antarctic, sea level, bedrock deformation, Earth system, climate change
Sea level change and ice sheet stability depend on how Earth’s bedrock warps as ice melts. Rock experiments show that traditional models for bedrock deformation leave out important processes relevant for modern ice loss. We simulate the coevolution of the Antarctic ice sheet and global sea level under various climate change scenarios. When more realistic bedrock behavior is considered, Antarctic ice retreat is delayed. Ultimately, this has implications for larger Earth system feedbacks.

item.title: Progress in high-resolution paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental reconstructions at two Upper Pleistocene key localities in the loess type region of the Upper and Middle Rhine area (Germany)
item.dc:creator: Peter Fischer, Markus Fuchs, Olaf Jöris, Frank Lehmkuhl, Olivier Le Moine, Charlotte Prud’homme, … (+1)
item.description:
Quaternary Research — matched: paleoclimate, interglacial, last interglacial, glacial cycle, Quaternary
In 1823/24 the term loess was introduced by Karl Caesar von Leonhard and its 200th anniversary was celebrated during the 2024 Loess Fest-conference in Mainz, Germany. Over these 200 years, loess research has evolved into a discipline of its own with initial approaches discussing the genesis and formation of this specific type of sediment, while later, the linkage to Quaternary climatic cycles was recognized. Nowadays, it is well known that loess–paleosol sequences (LPS) represent highly complex paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental archives with great spatial extent in the terrestrial realm covering the entire Quaternary. Here we present the state of research for two LPS in von Leonhard’s eponym region that evolved to key sections for the last interglacial–glacial cycle during the last decades: Schwalbenberg in the Middle Rhine valley and Nussloch in the Upper Rhine area. We demonstrate that these sites contribute to a better understanding of the mechanisms controlling the interplay of sediment accumulation, soil formation, sediment relocation, and associated preservation of climate signals in LPS. Furthermore, methodological advances allow for reconstruction of paleoenvironmental and paleoclimatic changes throughout the Upper Pleistocene on millennial- to centennial-scale resolution, highlighting the sensitivity of western European LPS to northern hemispheric climate oscillations.

item.title: Snow Phenology over Antarctic Sea Ice and Its Lagged Relationship with Sea Ice Thickness
item.dc:creator: zhihai chen, Ziwei Shao, Haoyuan Dang, Wenzheng Wang, Sixu Lu, Yueqian Cao, … (+1)
item.category: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
item.description:
Journal of Marine Science and Engineering — matched: Antarctic, surface mass balance, sea ice, neural network
Snow over Antarctic sea ice influences surface energy exchange, sea-ice growth, and surface mass balance, yet its seasonal evolution remains poorly understood due to sparse observations and uncertainties among retrieval methods. The timing of Antarctic sea-ice transitions has also exhibited substantial regional variability, raising the need to understand how snow phenology evolves with sea-ice conditions. Here, monthly snow-depth reconstructions from three deep-learning frameworks, including a convolutional neural network (CNN), the Kolmogorov–Arnold network (KAN), and multilayer perceptron (MLP), are used to characterize Antarctic snow phenology, including snow-onset month, snow-melt month, snow-season length, and annual maximum snow depth. Spatial trends of phenological metrics are quantified, and lagged relationships between snow depth and sea-ice thickness (SIT) are examined across 0–5 month lags. All three reconstruction frameworks reproduce the dominant seasonal cycle of Antarctic snow depth, characterized by reduced accumulation during austral summer and enhanced accumulation during winter and spring. The derived phenological metrics exhibit pronounced regional variability, with model differences most evident in snow-melt timing and snow-season length. Trend patterns reveal spatially heterogeneous changes rather than a uniform circumpolar response. Correlations between monthly snow-depth and SIT anomalies are strongest at short lags and decrease with increasing temporal offsets, showing that their monthly departures are most closely aligned over short intervals. The spread among reconstructions highlights the influence of model-dependent uncertainty on derived snow-phenology indicators and emphasizes the importance of multi-model assessments for interpreting Antarctic snow–ice coupling.

item.title: A record of polyphase Middle Pleistocene glaciation in the Sudetic Foreland, SW Poland
item.dc:creator: Dariusz Krzyszkowski, Lucyna Wachecka‐Kotkowska, Krzysztof Urbański, Elżbieta Myśkow, Marcin Krawczyk, Kaleb G. Wagner, … (+6)
item.description:
Quaternary Research — matched: ice sheet, Fennoscandian, MIS stage, cosmogenic
The Sudetic Foreland of Central Europe preserves an important sedimentary archive for reconstructing Pleistocene dynamics of the Scandinavian Ice Sheet, although the timing and character of pre-Saalian glaciations remain poorly constrained. This study presents an integrated sedimentological, structural, petrographic, and geochronological investigation of glaciogenic deposits exposed at the Jaźwina gravel pit. Two litho-petrographically distinct till units (T1 and T2) record changes in sediment provenance linked to the South Polish Complex (Elsterian1/2; MIS12/16). Glaciotectonic mesostructures indicate deformation under WNW–ESE-directed compression, interpreted as the combined effect of ice loading and reactivation of the Sudetic Marginal Fault. 10 Be– 26 Al burial dating of Fennoscandian erratics from the lower T1 till constrains its maximum depositional age to 620 ± 480 ka. Macrofossil wood remains (Quercus sp., Abies sp.) beneath the glacial succession are interpreted as redeposited from Early Pleistocene fluvial sediments. The combination of deformed tills, variable provenance signatures, and overprinted ice-flow indicators supports a polyphase glacial history involving thrust stacking of Middle Pleistocene deposits and subsequent tectonically driven denudation of the uppermost MIS 6 (Uciechów) till. These findings provide the first direct cosmogenic-nuclide age constraints for Middle Pleistocene tills and underscore the value of site-specific studies for resolving pre-Saalian glacial chronologies in Central Europe.

item.title: Glacier Albedo Variability During Transportation Infrastructure Construction: A Case Study of the Tianshan Shengli Tunnel
item.dc:creator: Yuhan Hu, Feiteng Wang, Weijun Mi, Fang Zhang, Ruiqi Pan, Jie Liu, … (+1)
item.description:
Remote Sensing — matched: glacier, albedo, proxy
Glacier surface albedo influences melt and may respond to climatic variability, changing surface conditions, and particulate emissions from nearby infrastructure. This study examined albedo variability across 434 glaciers near the Tianshan Shengli Tunnel during 2018–2024 using MODIS MOD10A1, Landsat 8/9 observations, ERA5 winds, and excavation records. Mean albedo during 2020–2024 was lower than during 2018–2019 by 0.025 for MODIS and 0.032 for Landsat. A distinct MODIS pixel-level quality-screening comparison applying an 80% daily valid-area coverage threshold yielded a descriptive difference of −0.0278. In the matched 357-glacier August–September sample, trends were −0.00597 yr−1 for the original masks and −0.00615 yr−1 after 60 m inward buffering; both 95% confidence intervals included zero. Cross-sensor observations covaried strongly (r = 0.867), although the bias of −0.073 and RMSE of 0.086 indicated substantial disagreement in magnitude. The climate-adjusted MODIS post-2020 coefficient was non-significant (−0.0190; p = 0.287), while the Landsat coefficient changed sign with trend specification. Across six excavation intervals, the construction-activity proxy showed a non-significant association with albedo anomalies (Spearman ρ = −0.543; exact p = 0.297), with direction sensitive to the reference baseline. Seasonal wind alignment described regional directional relationships but did not establish particle transport or deposition. The observations document lower later-period albedo and a negative interior-mask trend tendency without isolating a construction contribution. These findings support continuous dust control during emission-generating activities and coordinated glacier, meteorological, and deposition monitoring.

item.title: Distinguishing dynamic and thermal effects of the Tibetan Plateau on the Asian dust cycle using regional climate modeling
item.dc:creator: Hui Sun, Xiaodong Liu
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: bifurcation, Earth system model, Earth system, regional climate model
The Tibetan Plateau (TP) has profound influence on the Asian dust cycle through dynamic and thermal effects, yet quantification of the impacts of these effects remains inadequate. This study employed the Regional Climate Model (RegCM4) to systematically quantify the impacts of the two effects of the TP on dust cycle across six major Asian deserts through numerical experiments. The simulated results revealed that the dynamic effect suppresses springtime dust emission in the Taklimakan Desert by more than 500 mg m −2 day −1 but enhances that considerably (by almost 300–500 mg m −2 day −1) over the Loess Plateau. The thermal effect intensifies summer dust activity in the Thar Desert (by 500 mg m −2 day −1) and the Qaidam Basin, and is closely linked to strong convection and monsoon flows. The dust loading of East Asia peaks in spring under the dominance of the dynamic effect of the TP, while that in South Asia peaks in summer, driven primarily by the thermal effect of the TP. The dust deposition patterns indicate that the dynamic effect inhibits dust accumulation in the Taklimakan Desert, but promotes deposition on the Loess Plateau. The thermal effect enhances dust deposition through monsoon-related changes in soil moisture. The dynamic effect alters near-surface winds via topographic channeling and jet stream bifurcation, while the thermal effect modulates boundary layer stability and the large-scale circulations. This quantitative study elucidated how the dual forcings of the TP dynamically shape the patterns of the Asian dust cycle, providing critical constraints for Earth System Models.

item.title: Boron isotopes in fluvial palaeochannels reveal catchment weathering and climate variability over the last glacial–interglacial cycle
item.dc:creator: Anthony Dosseto, Christian Ercolani, Damien Lemarchand
item.description:
Quaternary Science Reviews — matched: interglacial
Boron (B) isotopes in fluvial clay fractions can provide information about catchment weathering and vegetation–soil interactions during past environmental change. We investigate clay- and sand-fraction B isotope compositions, clay B/Al ratios, mineralogy and neodymium isotopes from 14 sites across four Murrumbidgee River palaeochannel systems in southeastern Australia, spanning the last glacial–interglacial cycle. Sampling position, mineralogical assemblages and geochemical observations are combined to assess potential post-depositional overprinting. Several shallow or exposed samples have elevated δ 11 B, consistent with interaction with isotopically heavy soil or pore waters. In the screened dataset, clay–sand isotope offsets (Δ 11 Bclay–sand) are relatively low in Yanco and Gum Creek sediments and more positive in Kerarbury, Coleambally and recent deposits. Overlapping εNd compositions provide no clear evidence for a systematic provenance shift among systems. The boron isotope contrasts, considered alongside regional vegetation records and clay mineralogy, suggest changes in the influence of biologically modified soil solutions on catchment weathering products. More positive offsets are consistent with greater vegetation-mediated B cycling, whereas lower offsets in the younger systems may reflect reduced biological processing, increased contributions from deeper regolith, or both. Published palaeohydrological evidence places these younger deposits within periods of enhanced fluvial activity, suggesting that greater water and sediment delivery coexisted with a reduced biological imprint on exported clays. The results demonstrate the potential of boron isotopes to complement fluvial and vegetation archives by tracing changes in catchment weathering regime, while emphasising the importance of assessing post-depositional preservation.

item.title: Diagnosing the Roles of Large-Scale Circulation in Tropical Precipitation Biases in CESM2 Using Nudging Technique
item.dc:creator: Fucheng Yang, Jie He, Boniface Fosu, Yen‐Heng Lin, Yi Deng, Honghai Zhang
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: Earth system model, Earth system, reanalysis, parameterization
Persistent tropical precipitation biases in general circulation models can arise from errors in both the large-scale environment and the subgrid-scale processes that produce precipitation, making their respective contributions difficult to isolate. Here, we evaluate precipitation in the Community Earth System Model version 2.2.2 (CESM2) using a revised nudging framework that constrains horizontal winds, specific humidity, and/or temperature toward reanalysis. Constraining horizontal winds substantially reduces climatological precipitation biases across the tropical Pacific, including dry biases over the western Pacific warm pool and northern Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and wet biases in the subtropics. Importantly, replacing the largescale circulation with reanalysis also shifts precipitation from overly frequent light rainfall toward heavier intensities, despite no modifications to the model’s moist physics parameterizations. This improvement is closely associated with reorganized moisture transport and more frequent strong moisture convergence events, even in regions where the climatological humidity does not increase. Further constraining specific humidity or temperature provides no systematic additional improvement, highlighting the central role of circulation in setting the environment to which moist physics parameterizations respond. However, regional biases remain, particularly an underestimation of heavy precipitation, even though model’s lower troposphere remains closer to saturation than in reanalysis during substantial precipitation events. Together, the substantial shift from overly frequent light rainfall toward heavier intensities under circulation constraint indicates that errors in the large-scale environment contribute importantly to precipitation biases in CESM2, while the remaining discrepancies likely also reflect limitations in the moist physics parameterizations.

item.title: Asynchronous seasonal velocity variations across Taku Glacier’s piedmont lobe
item.dc:creator: Lynn M. Kaluzienski, J. M. Amundson, Ian R. Joughin, Shin Sugiyama, Arlec Chang
item.description:
Journal of Glaciology — matched: subglacial, glacier
Taku Glacier recently started to retreat after advancing several kilometers through a deep fjord during the 20th century. The glacier currently features a 6.1-km-wide piedmont lobe that is protected from the ocean by a subaerial moraine that formed during its advance. Satellite-derived velocity fields and Global Navigation Satellite System measurements reveal asynchronous seasonal velocity variations across the lobe. The eastern side exhibits a typical ‘spring speedup’ with peak velocities in March, while the western side reaches peak velocities in July. Historical imagery shows that the western side overrode a substantial sediment outwash plain during advance, aligning with the region of late-season velocity peaks, whereas the eastern side advanced through deep water with presumably less sediment. We propose that the distinct velocity patterns reflect spatial differences in subglacial drainage efficiency: the drainage system on the eastern side appears to seasonally transition from an inefficient, distributed network to an efficient, channelized network, while the drainage system on the western side appears to remain (relatively) inefficient year round. Our findings suggest that glaciers with year-round inefficient drainage may experience larger seasonal velocity variations than those that establish efficient drainage in summer because high, sustained water fluxes do not cause subglacial water pressures to drop during summer.

item.title: Historical and future climate niche of Colombian glaciers: A multi-statistical analysis
item.dc:creator: Maria Paula Rivera Reyes, Adriana Sanchez, Alvaro Avila-Diaz, Jorge L. Ceballos, Benjamin Quesada
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: glacier, mass loss, climate change
by Maria Paula Rivera Reyes, Adriana Sanchez, Alvaro Avila-Diaz, Jorge L. Ceballos, Benjamin Quesada Since the mid-20th century, tropical glacier recession has accelerated, but substantial uncertainty remains regarding their disappearence timing. In Colombia, only six glacierized areas remain between 11° N and 2° N, and most of the country’s glacier cover has already disappeared. Developing novel and integrative methods for predicting glacier retreat and understanding the climatic drivers of glacier change is therefore critical for anticipating future water availability and ecosystem responses in high-mountain regions. In this study, we innovatively used the Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) model to estimate the potential distribution of glaciers in Sierra Nevada El Cocuy (the largest extent) and Santa Isabel (lowest extent) in Colombia, under multiple climate-change scenarios and time periods. We also used multilinear models to analyze in-situ glacier mass-balance records with climate data from Terra to identify the most influential climatic drivers of glacier mass loss. Our results indicate that Santa Isabel glacier and El Cocuy glacier are projected to lose up to 90% of their suitable area by 2021–2040 and 2040–2060, respectively, under high-emission scenarios. The importance of climatic variables in glacier distribution differs between sites. For Cocuy, temperature of the wettest quarter (48%) and precipitation of the driest quarter (48%) were most relevant variables, while for Santa Isabel, temperature of the driest quarter dominated (92%). In situ mass-balance records show that temperature is the dominant driver of glacier mass loss at both locations (45–65%), which is concerning given that temperature increases across Colombia are unequivocal in all climate projections. Wind, solar radiation, and precipitation further modulate glacier response in site-specific ways, with a more prominent role at El Cocuy. These findings highlight the urgent need to expand glaciological and climate monitoring and provide an integrated analytical approach with potential applicability in other mountain regions, subject to regional characteristics and data availability.

item.title: Eurasian–North American Hot Extremes: Intercontinental Covariability and Associated Physical Mechanisms
item.dc:creator: Bin Yu, Hai Lin, Dingrui Cao
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: sea surface temperature, reanalysis, heat wave
This study examines the intercontinental covariability of summer heatwave-related hot extremes between Eurasia and North America using 66 years (1959–2024) of ERA5 reanalysis and observational data. Hot extremes are quantified using the warm extreme index (TX90), and maximum covariance analysis (MCA) identifies three leading modes that collectively explain nearly 80% of the squared covariance between the two continents. Each mode exhibits coherent circumglobal teleconnection patterns linking major hot-extreme regions across Eurasia and North America. Dynamical analyses reveal that these modes are associated with quasi-stationary zonal wavenumber-5 Rossby wave trains, maintained by synoptic eddy forcing and barotropic interactions along the midlatitude jet, providing an efficient pathway for intercontinental teleconnections. Thermodynamically, TX90 variability is dominated by surface radiative processes, with downward shortwave radiation regulated by cloud cover and downward longwave radiation influenced by lower-tropospheric temperature and water vapor anomalies. Near-surface air temperature anomalies reinforce extreme heat conditions, while cloud-related radiative effects partly offset them; surface turbulent heat fluxes play a secondary, mode-dependent role. Sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies contribute weakly, with tropical Pacific cooling indicating secondary tropical–extratropical coupling and midlatitude SST anomalies largely reflecting atmospheric forcing. Spectral analyses further highlight contributions from interannual variability and decadal-to-multidecadal circulation shifts. Overall, these results indicate that Northern Hemisphere summer hot extremes across distant regions are organized by a coupled dynamical–thermodynamic framework, in which intercontinental covariability is driven primarily by atmospheric dynamical linkages, while local land-surface radiative feedbacks amplify extremes regionally and surface radiative heating sustains their intensity.

item.title: Gender differentiated livelihood vulnerability to climate change and variability: Experience of rural households in northern Ethiopia
item.dc:creator: Fentahun Gebrie Mucha, Zerihun Yohannes Amare, Solomon Addisu Legesse
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: climate change, IPCC
by Fentahun Gebrie Mucha, Zerihun Yohannes Amare, Solomon Addisu Legesse Climate change disproportionately affects economically and socially disadvantaged groups, where differences in livelihood vulnerability frequently intensified by gender inequalities, although empirical evidence remains limited. The vulnerability of rural households’ livelihoods to climate change is influenced by socioeconomic and biophysical contexts; however, the assessment of gendered vulnerability remains limited in northern Ethiopia. This study aimed to examine rural households’ livelihood vulnerability to climate change and variability through a gender lens. Employing a mixed research approach with a concurrent design, data collection was carried out through household surveys, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and field observations. A multistage sampling technique was employed to choose the sample households, and the Livelihood Vulnerability Index based on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (LVI-IPCC) framework, which assesses vulnerability through exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity, was used to analyze of livelihood vulnerability. Data were collected from 396 surveyed households, six focus group discussions and nine key informants. The findings from the LVI-IPCC indicate a statistically significant gender difference in livelihood vulnerability. Female-headed households (FHHs) show higher vulnerability (0.098) compared to male-headed households (MHHs) (0.061), primarily attributed to higher sensitivity (0.550) and lower adaptive capacity (0.380). However, MHHs show lower sensitivity (0.507) and greater adaptive capacity (0.491). Nevertheless, no significant gender difference was found in the exposure component. These findings underline the necessity for targeted and gender-transformative interventions to strengthen the adaptive capacity of FHHs by improving access to agricultural technologies, climate information services, skill development, livelihood diversification opportunities, and financial services, including inclusive microfinance.

item.title: An Optimized Protocol for Black Carbon Extraction from Lacustrine Sedimentary Rocks
item.dc:creator: Yanjun Bao, Yuanyuan Sun, Lin Ding, Bin Zhou, Yuxin He, Wei Sun, … (+10)
item.description:
Analytical Chemistry — matched: paleoclimate, proxy
The black carbon (BC) concentration and carbon isotopic composition (δ13C) are critical proxies for identifying C3/C4 vegetation and reconstructing fire history, offering valuable insights into paleoclimate and paleoecology. Among the various analytical techniques for BC extraction, chemical oxidation is the most widely applied approach for isolating BC from soils, modern sediments, and marine sedimentary rocks. However, its application to lacustrine sedimentary rocks remains limited, and the reliability of using BC signatures to reconstruct fire history and vegetation evolution in inland regions has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we selected Cenozoic lacustrine mudstone samples from the Tibetan Plateau to evaluate and enhance the reliability and stability of chemical oxidation methods for BC extraction from such archives. Our results indicate that prolonging the oxidation duration to ≥120 h is essential for isolating refractory BC while preserving the original carbon isotopic signal. Furthermore, extending the hydrofluoric acid (HF) treatment time to 36 h removes silicate minerals more thoroughly. Using the optimized protocol, BC was extracted from paleolake sediments in the Qaidam and Zhada basins. Morphological, molecular, and elemental analyses suggest that the isolated BC is predominantly derived from biomass combustion, with negligible contributions from graphite minerals, kerogen, or graphitized carbon. This approach offers a practical framework that may help improve the reliability of BC analysis in lacustrine sedimentary rocks. It also supports the use of BC carbon content and δ13C analysis in paleofire and vegetation reconstruction, with potential implications for paleoclimate and paleoecology research on the Tibetan Plateau and other inland regions.

item.title: Orographic and Thermal Regulation of Quasi-biweekly Summer Rainfall over Southeastern China by the Tibetan Plateau
item.dc:creator: Guanshun Zhang, Jiangyu Mao, Jianying Li, Bian He, Yimin Liu, Sheng Hu, … (+2)
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: model intercomparison, reanalysis
Using multi-year observational and reanalysis data along with simulations from the Global Monsoon Model Intercomparison Project, this study disentangles the distinct yet complementary roles of the orographic and thermal forcings of the Tibetan Plateau (TP) in regulating downstream quasi-biweekly oscillation (QBWO) of summer rainfall and the resultant persistent heavy rainfall (PHR) over southeastern China. The QBWO involves the synergistic interactions of atmospheric potential vorticity (PV) anomalies originating from the eastern TP (ETP) and the northern South China Sea–East China Sea (SECS) regions, with the ETP-derived PV propagating southeastward while the SECS-derived PV moving northwestward to jointly amplify the vertically-coupled PV dipole over southeastern China. Dynamically, the TP's orographic forcing creates PV anomalies in the lower troposphere due to lateral friction curl resulting from anomalous flows around the TP, forming a vertically-coupled PV dipole over the ETP following the thermal wind relationship. The TP thus acts as a "signal amplifier" that facilitates phase-locking of the upper-tropospheric quasi-biweekly wave train, thereby governing downstream rainfall intensity. In contrast, the TP’s surface thermal forcing reshapes the South Asian high and its northern-flank westerly waveguide, altering the propagation pattern of the upper-tropospheric wave train and the amplitude of PV anomalies over southeastern China, with a certain modulation effect on the QBWO frequency. Simulations show that removing the TP's topography or thermal forcing reduces the downstream convective intensity by 22.1% or 43.8%, respectively. These two forcing mechanisms collectively determine the QBWO evolution and PHR occurrence over southeastern China, providing mechanistic support for improving intraseasonal PHR predictions.

item.title: Finding commonalities and sharing results effectively are imperative for co-creative decolonial Arctic research
item.dc:creator: Susanna Gartler, Ria-Maria Adams, Sophie Elixhauser, Charleen Fisher, Ellen Marie Jensen, Simon Jungblut, … (+3)
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: Arctic
by Susanna Gartler, Ria-Maria Adams, Sophie Elixhauser, Charleen Fisher, Ellen Marie Jensen, Simon Jungblut, Hugues Lantuit, Alexandra Meyer, Gertrude Saxinger In recent years, Arctic Indigenous Peoples have articulated clear guidelines for equitable research practices. However, two interconnected aspects warrant greater attention: identifying commonalities and sharing research results. Research must be grounded in shared goals established through co-creative processes between Arctic communities and scientists. Based on these commonalities, scientific results must be shared effectively and continuously with communities, requiring knowledge-sharing to be embedded in funding schemes and project designs.

item.title: The Shift from Dry to Warm Dominance in Snow Drought on the Tibetan Plateau
item.dc:creator: Ye Jiang, Tao Che, Liyun Dai, Xuemei Li, Dongdong Feng
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: albedo, climate change
Under climate change, the warming and shortening of the cold season have led to substantial snow-cover loss on the Tibetan Plateau, resulting in widespread and severe snow drought. This reduction in snow cover diminishes the plateau’s capacity to regulate water resources and further amplifies regional warming by altering surface albedo and energy balance. This study investigates the spatiotemporal dynamics of snow drought on the Tibetan Plateau during 1988–2023, with a focus on shifts among dry, warm, and warm-dry snow drought types. The results show that, from 1988 to 2023, snow droughts increased in both spatial extent and severity, accompanied by a gradual transition from dry snow droughts to warm and warm-dry types. Elevation analysis reveals a rising prevalence of warm snow droughts, while dry snow droughts have declined at all altitudes, with the most pronounced contrast occurring at 4500–5500 m. Areas below 3500 m, where both affected extent and drought intensity have increased, emerge as hotspots of changing snow drought risk. Seasonally, dry snow droughts contract in autumn but intensify locally, expand and strengthen in winter, and weaken in both extent and intensity in spring. In contrast, warm and warm-dry snow droughts remain more widespread and severe across all seasons. These findings provide important insights into the changing snow drought regime on the Tibetan Plateau and its implications for hydrology and ecosystems.

item.title: GEOS-Chem-hyd: enabling source-oriented sensitivity analysis with GEOS-Chem
item.dc:creator: Samuel O. Akinjole, Jiachen Liu, Shannon L. Capps
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: sensitivity analysis
Air pollution degrades human health and public welfare. Quantifying the impacts of diverse sources of air pollution is challenging. Simulations are helpful for understanding these complex interactions and end points. With this development, a well-regarded simulation of air pollutants may now trace where pollution from a selected source goes around the world and what happens to it chemically when it is released into the atmosphere. This augmented model may help scientists and decisionmakers.

item.title: A differentiable framework for general circulation model precipitation bias correction
item.dc:creator: Kamlesh Sawadekar, Seth McGinnis, Peijun Li, Kathryn Lawson, Chaopeng Shen
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: machine learning
Global climate models are essential for planning, but their rainfall predictions contain systematic errors that limit local use. We built a correction tool that uses machine learning to choose the settings of a simple, interpretable formula rather than producing corrected rainfall directly. Tested across the United States, it corrected typical and heavy rainfall well, kept realistic spatial patterns, partly preserved future trends, and showed promise in regions it had never seen.

item.title: Redistribution of frost weathering across Spain under recent climate warming
item.dc:creator: Carlos Gabriel Morales, María Teresa Ortega, Javier Martínez-Martínez
item.description:
The Cryosphere
We analyzed 30 years of daily records from 84 Spanish weather stations to assess evolving freezing and thawing patterns and cryoclastic indices. While freezing activity is concentrated in mountain regions and minimal in lowlands, trends reveal a general decline. Crucially, some high-altitude belts retain sustained, intense activity. Projections to 2050 indicate a progressive altitudinal restriction of effective freezing conditions, with significant implications for geomorphic processes.
